utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances at the 25th session of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic with Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything special, any administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's proceed directly with Witness Number 35. Thank you for the proofing notes. They are available also for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Is anybody prepared to bring the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, can we please hear your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just to remind you, I know you speak English, but please wait for the interpretation to be complete before answering and pause a moment before answering only in your language. Doctor, can you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: My name is Mirsad, Mirsad [as interpreted] Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, where were you born and in what year?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I was born in Banja Luka in 1962.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I grew up in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what your education was and where you were educated?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I completed my elementary and secondary education in Prijedor after which I went to study university in Banja Luka. I completed graduate studies -- postgraduate studies in Zagreb, and I began my specialisation in surgery in Bihac and completed it in Sarajevo. But I spent part of my specialisation training in Ljubljana, also in Vienna, in Austria and Munich and Freyberg in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct that your profession is a medical doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I am a medical doctor, a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you continuing to practice medicine today?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I was always involved in my actual profession, and that is -- this is what I did for most of my life, and I still practice, as a plastic surgeon actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- can you tell the Court about where you worked after completing your medical training? First, what year did you complete your medical training?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school of medicine in 1987. Thereupon, I continued working as a general practitioner in the town of Prijedor until 1990. Actually, 1991, to be more precise. And it was at that time that I started my specialisation in general surgery. And after the war broke out, I fled to Bihac and continued my training in general surgery there. As for my qualifications as a surgeon, I can provide you with more details. I studied in Sarajevo, Ljubljana, Germany, Austria, also in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you worked in the town of Prijedor. Did you only work within the town of Prijedor, or did you ever work in other parts of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: There were two so-called primary medical institutions in Prijedor. One of them covered the nonworking community, nonworking residents, and they were distributed in various neighbourhoods and villages of the municipality of Prijedor. The second segment, the second institution, covered the working population, and this was the so-called occupational medicine institution. Such surgeries, there were several of them, were located throughout the town of Prijedor, but they were always linked to a particular company or a working organisation. So through my working experience, I was able to become familiar with the entire town of Prijedor and had contacts -- numerous contacts with various segments of the population through my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, the interpretation indicated that you became familiar with the town of Prijedor and worked in the town. I'm not sure, are you saying that you only worked within the town, or did you work in other parts of the Opstina or municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: When I said the town of Prijedor, I was actually referring to the municipality of Prijedor because in our language and in the way we speak, we often confuse the two, the two concepts, the town and the municipality. I actually had opportunity to work in the entire municipality of Prijedor, not only the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do compulsory military service in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In 1980 and 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your job when you were doing your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: During my military service, I was with the communications Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. department, with the signals, in infantry units. I was a simple infantry soldier, but I was later sent to undergo officers' training, which I completed in the rank of sergeant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that point after you completed your officer training, is it correct that you worked within a medical unit within the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As for the medical corps, at that period of time, I'm talking about my generation and one generation before me, we were sent -- we were required to do our military service immediately after completing the secondary education. And that is why I served outside the medical corps of the army. Prior to my generation, conscripts went to do their military service only after they completed their university education. So graduates of medicine were used for that purpose while doing their compulsory military service. But since I served immediately after completing my secondary education, I was just a soldier with the infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a soldier with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, I was never a soldier of the BH army, though it may sound paradoxical, because many people ask me how come I served the JNA and not the BH army later on. No, no, I was never a member of the BH army. Throughout the war, I worked as a physician, as a medical doctor, and I never donned a uniform. I spent that entire period of time wearing a white uniform, a doctor's white coat, and I performed my duties in accordance with the ethics of the medical profession. I provided assistance to Serbs, Croats, Muslims alike, to anybody who needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Doctor, is your -- are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am married, and I have three children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of your wife?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: She is also a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your first two children, can you just tell us what year they were born in?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: My eldest son was born in 1987. My younger son was born in October 1991. So prior to the beginning of the war, my eldest son was four, and the youngest one was six months old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any other party other than the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. After the democratic changes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I became a member of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how it was that you came to become a member of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Personally, my motive for joining the party was to make my own contribution to the democratic changes which were taking place in our country at the time. And although I did not consider it as my vocation, politics. I was already a student of graduate studies in Zagreb at the time, and I always considered myself as a scientist, not as a politician. But despite that fact, at that time, I felt that it was necessary for me to join in this process of transformation because I felt that there was a kind of revolution going on, a democratic revolution, going on. The previous system, the communism, we had had it for about 50 years, and I felt that it was necessary for me to join and to make my contribution to these democratic changes in the society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which individual or individuals first approached you about joining the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Nijaz Kapetanovic. He was one of the founding members of the party, together with several other individuals. At that time, the party had already had its steering committee established, and they asked me to help find a larger group of intellectuals and to mobilise them so as to have the party enriched in this sense as well. And I took it upon myself to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that at the time you joined, I think you indicated at one point you were doing some training in Zagreb. Can you explain, did you join the party in Zagreb, or in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I joined the party in Prijedor. There were no such activities in Zagreb at the time. At least, I don't remember that there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you at this time still travelling or living part-time in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, I spent most of my time in Prijedor even while I was a postgraduate student, but I would go to the university during my leave, my annual leave, and my paid leave of absence, which used to be the custom for those who were undergoing some additional training. So I spent 80 per cent of my time in Prijedor, and about 20 per cent of my time in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your parents live in Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife and children -- excuse me. Where did your wife and children live at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Also in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife have a profession?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did. She is also a physician, and we were together postgraduate students.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the interpretation finish? I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hold any position within the SDA in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I became president of the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how that happened? Was there an election or how were you chosen?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As I said, there was this initiative committee or steering committee which had about 50 members, mostly volunteers, most of whom I did not know. So I didn't expect much, in terms of being elected to any of the functions. At that time, there were two currents within this board, each of them supported their own candidate. Nijaz Kapetanovic and several other members then lobbied for myself as some kind of medium -- midway solution in order to reconcile the two currents that existed within the board. So without any previous experience or knowledge, I was elected to this position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you at that time that you were elected the president of the SDA in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later hold a position within a region of which Prijedor is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a part?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I became the president of the regional board, the region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that region include various municipalities that were part of the Bosanska Krajina, SDA committees from various municipalities part of the Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It consisted of 17 municipalities of the Bosniak Krajina, that is the region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever elected to a position, an elected position not within the party but within the government or legislature?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was nominated to the House of Citizens at the election, and I was elected deputy to the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how the legislature of Bosnia and Herzegovina was set up. Was it one unicameral or a bicameral legislature?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The legislature of Bosnia-Herzegovina had two Chambers. The Chamber of Citizens and the Chamber of Municipalities. The Chamber of Citizens had 130 deputies which were elected according to the relevant regions and the Chamber of Municipalities had 110 deputies which were elected on the basis of municipalities. Each municipality elected their representative to the Chamber of Municipalities in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what jurisdiction were you elected in? Which area did you represent?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Chamber of Citizens is a legislative body which approved, or rather, drafted proposals to legal documents together with the government. It had jurisdiction over all proposals or drafts at the level of the republic. And they initiated proposals of bills which were to be passed or approved at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question is: What is the electorate, the area, that voted in the election in which you were elected? Is it for the Opstina of Prijedor or was it on a national level or regional level?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Chamber of Citizens was elected in the following way: There were seven regions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And depending on the size of the region, a certain number of deputies were to be elected. As far as the Bosnian Krajina is concerned, there were 25 deputies to be elected. And it all depended on the number of votes that the relevant party received during the election. So the House of Citizens, the Chamber of Citizens, its members were elected on the basis of the so-called regional principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you elect as a member of a particular party on a particular list, and if so, can you explain how that list is made up?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: When I indicated that I was the president of the regional board, I did not mean to say that I was elected to the office of the president of the regional board. The nature of this function was a coordinative one, and it happened as a result of a number of coincidences, because the town of Prijedor had the majority of Bosniak population. And it was actually the town of Prijedor which deserved this function, not myself personally, so I was acting as the president of the regional board which drafted the list of candidates for the Chamber of Citizens at the regional level. And during one of these sessions, I was nominated as the first person on the list of SDA party members for the Chamber of Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the parliament in Bosnia, did that give you public exposure? Was there any way for the average people to know what was going on in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: All sessions of the parliament were broadcast directly through the media. There was TV coverage for all parliament sessions. So it was through my work and my appearances in the parliament that the public of Bosnia and Herzegovina had the opportunity to become familiar with my person and work. The same goes for many other deputies, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the ethnic makeup of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put S1 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being prepared, Witness, Doctor, can you tell us what was the breakdown in the population according to the 1991 census in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: According to the 1991 census, there were 44 per cent Bosniaks, 42.5 per cent Serbs, 5.5 per cent Croats, the remaining citizens of Prijedor belonged to other ethnic groups, Bosnians, Bosniaks, Yugoslavs. In the village of Trnopolje, there were other nationalities, other ethnic groups, too. There were 17 different minorities in Trnopolje of different origins, Czech, Ukrainian, German, Hungarian, and so on and so forth, 17 different minorities, different minorities of European origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you is S1 on the screen in front of you, and as you can see it is colour-coded to indicate the predominant ethnic group in various settlements, towns, and municipalities. Do you find this to be roughly accurate as to how the ethnicities were distributed within Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Essentially, as far as I can tell, shown here on this map are only certain points marking certain villages inhabited by Croats, Serbs, or Bosniaks. But this way of presenting it is just not accurate enough because the areas are not marked with precision, the areas in which citizens of certain nationality live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that there are also minorities in many of these areas, that they're not pure -- can you explain, please. How were the ethnicities distributed? Was it one pure ethnicity in various areas or were there areas where they were intermixed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: This is the essence of what I tried to say. This map is oversimplified. For example, it shows Ljubija marked in green, which would probably mean that only Bosniaks lived there, but that's not true. In Ljubija, there was a small percentage, minor percentage of both Croats and Serbs, whereas on the other hand, in the village of Trnopolje, there also lived a number of Serbs and other ethnic groups, too. All, for example, in a number of villages such as Brezicani. Brezicani had a Serb majority and a Muslim minority. Therefore, there were a number of villages where citizens of all three ethnic groups were mixed, which is not really shown clearly on this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a difference between how people lived and ethnicities were mixed within the town and the area surrounding the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: There was no essential major difference in the way of life. There was a difference in terms of certain historic indications. Kozarac, for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. example, until the 1960s, was a municipality, as well as Ljubija, well into the 1960s. And Prijedor was, in a way, on the same level as Kozarac and Ljubija. But Kozarac and Ljubija, their citizens, they've always had their own identity, very keenly felt. This especially is true of the citizens of Kozarac. Kozarac, as a town, was established as a town in the 13th century, a long time before Prijedor, which was established in the 17th century. Omarska itself is also a separate entity in a way. It had not been a municipality before, but due to the high concentration of Serbian population in this area, there were over 20.000 citizens of Serb nationality there, it was also displaying certain aspirations to become a municipality in its own right. So that Prijedor was a agglomerate of a number of different, let me say, entities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the outbreak of the conflict in 1992 in Prijedor, were people affect, in your view, by memories of historical events in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: From the historical point of view, until 1942, Prijedor was controlled by the so-called Ustasha government. This was the government of the independent state of Croatia and its dictator, Ante Pavelic. It was a time in which particularly the Serb peoples suffered a great deal of damage and loss of lives, especially from Potkozarje. Many Serbs from Potkozarje perished in the camp at Jasenovac. So that the way Serbs from the region perceived the situation from a position full of pain in terms of Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a difference in the history of various parts of Prijedor and the role they played, these various areas, in the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: When I spoke about Serbs, Serb citizens in Prijedor and their sufferings, what I was mostly referring to was citizens of Serb nationality who lived in the area of the Kozara mountain, the so-called Potkozarje, which is an area traditionally with a partisan past. And this area was a symbol in the former Yugoslavia, in Tito's Yugoslavia, of brotherhood and unity, a symbol which Ante Markovic used, when he sensed that Yugoslavia was in crisis, to found his own party and to point out, to underline the importance of this epic or mythical, if you like, area of Potkozarje. Known, famous, throughout the former Yugoslavia, even songs from the area were sung throughout Yugoslavia. On the other hand, we have the Omarska area, where there was also a high concentration of Serbs. Historically speaking, this area had a Chetnik past, marked by Chetnik ideology basing itself on Draza Mihajlovic's ideology, which was to blame for many crimes against non-Serb population during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the results of the 1991 census. Did this census indicate any trend in changes in the population percentages of the various ethnicities? In other words, how did it compare to earlier census results?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The 1991 census showed a completely different picture of the proportions, of the ratio between the different ethnic groups in Prijedor, so that in 1981 apparently, there were 43 per cent Serbs, 38 per cent Bosniaks, 6 per cent Croats, and citizens belonging to other ethnic groups, or of other identities and allegations that I've mentioned before. So the main difference between the 1981 and 1991 census is that in the 1991 [as interpreted] Census, the Serbs were an obvious majority. There were 5 per cent more Serbs than Bosniaks, whereas according to the 1991 census, the overall picture was reversed so that the Bosniaks suddenly became the majority. And the Serbs the minority, but the difference is not that great. It really -- it's really a bit more than 1 per cent. In absolute figures, this is 49.700 Bosniaks and 48.000 Serbs, which means -- which implies a difference of only 1.700 citizens in favour of Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, without going into great detail regarding history, can you tell us, at the time that you became the president of the SDA in Prijedor, were the surrounding events involving changes in Yugoslavia, did they have an effect in Prijedor, and can you briefly describe what the main issues were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: These changes date back to 1987, the changes within the Communist Party. First in Serbia and then throughout Yugoslavia. The splitting up of the system according to a national principle, first Slovenia bailed out, and then Croatia, and the Bosnian delegation distanced itself. Then the appearance, the emergence of Milosevic as an undisputed leader in Serbia, and then his later political behaviour, his public statements. He appeared as the guardian of Serbs throughout Yugoslavia. And as the herald of an idea that was to divide the whole of Yugoslavia against Milosevic, pro and against Milosevic. The essence of his idea was to abolish the 1974 constitution, which afforded equal rights to all federal units regardless of their size. So a republic as small as Montenegro with only 600.000 inhabitants had the same number of delegates, the same number of votes, in the federal parliament as Serbia with 8 million people. This principle, however, guaranteed equality to all ethnic groups, a principle founded by Tito, and up to that point always respected, observed. Milosevic wanted to change this principle by introducing a new principle, one citizen, one vote, whereby he could gain the upper hand in the former Yugoslavia because Serbs were the majority ethnic group. This was unacceptable to all other ethnic groups and resulted later on in the disintegration of Yugoslavia. What is essential for the case of Prijedor is that their situation was very much reflected in Prijedor, and Prijedor was carved up into the two opposing camps, the pro-Milosevic and the contra-Milosevic camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which political parties belonged to the pro-Milosevic and which to the anti-Milosevic camps?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, even the communist party itself split up into a number of anti-Milosevic factions. So that a number of organisations within the communist party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, depending on what the majority was in that particular region, Bosniak, Serb, or Croat, these factions were also divided along ethnic lines, pro and contra, pro- and anti-Milosevic. If talking about parties based on a certain national zeal such as the Party of Democratic Action, the Croatian Democratic Union or Serbian Democratic Party, speaking of these, it is clear that the SDS backed Milosevic, gave him full support, as well as other Serb parties founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina such as the Serbian Movement of Reconstruction based on Vuk Draskovic's ideology in Serbia, or the Radical Party, only established in Prijedor, in Omarska, whereas on the other hand, part of the communist association, the then Social Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Democratic Party, Party of Democratic Action, and the HDZ were against this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was the SDA platform against Yugoslavia at the time of its founding?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: In the part of the founding programme of the SDA was the preservation of Yugoslavia as an essential element for the survival of Bosniaks in these areas. So the SDA viewed the problem of Yugoslavia in the same way as all the other republics and all the other citizens of Yugoslavia who tended to see Yugoslavia as a community of all the different ethnic groups with equal rights for all. But they decidedly opposed Milosevic's vision of Yugoslavia which offered no such equality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect of the Slovene and Croatian declarations of independence upon the platform of SDA and its willingness to stay within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The SDA cherished a theory of equidistance as Bosnia-Herzegovina was multinational already in terms of its ethnic makeup. And by that very fact had to observe a balance between Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats. When Slovenia and Croatia began to drift away from the former Yugoslavia, the attitude of the SDA was: If Croatia stays as part of the former Yugoslavia, we shall still consider that country as Yugoslavia, if only Slovenia decides to leave and Croatia stays, because there will continue to exist a balance between Croatia on the one side and Serbia on the other. If Croatia should leave, too, secede from the former Yugoslavia, then the balance is clearly compromised and that is no longer Yugoslavia, but rather the Greater Serbia. Our attitude was that in that case, we couldn't be left behind as only part of Greater Serbia and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the war following the Croatian declaration of independence in 1991, did that war have its effects upon Prijedor, and if so, can you explain those.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia was a warning to the citizens of Prijedor. It meant that the terrors of war could also spread to the Prijedor area, and the citizens were wary of such a possibility, especially because we had this analysis by a Slovene expert named Gersak, saying that it was exactly precisely in the Prijedor area, due to its strategic importance and position and its proximity to Banja Luka, there could be conflicts and clashes in the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did mobilisations occur within Prijedor, and did this have some effect upon the populations?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the war began in Croatia, the JNA wanted to mobilise all citizens of Prijedor. There was an instruction from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that its citizens should not take part in this war against Croatia and against Croats. It was considered as fratricide, and they were advised not to respond to mobilisation or to callups to take part in this war against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the time that you had served in the JNA during your compulsory military service until the outbreak of the conflict in 1992, had the JNA changed? And if so, can you explain those changes.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The JNA, at the time when I was serving my military service, that was in the 1980s, early 1980, 1981, the army was Yugoslav in the true sense of the word. It reflected the interests of all the ethnic groups, all the nationalities living in the former Yugoslavia. There were several elements showing this. I will only name the most important ones. Above all, high positions in the army such as generals, in the 1980s, there were about six Bosnian generals and an equal ratio, a proportional ratio of all other nationalities, too, Croats, Slovenes. This was gradually lost so that in the 1990s, there was not a single Bosnian general. And in the JNA, also other ethnic groups lost a number of generals. So gradually, in a gradual way, the army became ever more Serbian and ever less Yugoslav, in the sense of the word I have just described. Another important problem that gave rise to a certain amount of mistrust by citizens from the other republics of Yugoslavia, other than Serbia, that is, is that in 1989, the internal organisation and structure of the JNA underwent thorough changes. Before, it was based mostly on the republican principal and responded within the republican borders of the former Yugoslavia. This new organisation scheme carved up the republics without observing their borders and created a unitarian organisation. Thirdly, a very important issue, they separated from the makeup of the JNA, units of the Territorial Defence. Those were, we can say, republican armies. Weapons were taken from their storage facilities and transferred to the storage facilities of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the events of the war in Croatia affect people's confidence in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Wartime events added to the citizens' lack of confidence, the Bosniak citizens, especially when speaking about Prijedor, because the mobilisation that was carried out the first time when two brigades from Prijedor were to be transferred into Croatia, the collection sites in Jaruge, there were several witnesses there, witnessing to the setting up of the 45th Kozarac Brigade, Colonel Colic was also there. There were many soldiers there wearing Chetnik insignia, which stunned many people into disbelief. They considered that this was untenable and unacceptable for the JNA. Obviously, Colonel Colic did not mind. What's more, on that occasion, he said that one should go to war in Croatia whereupon, a major number of mobilised soldiers, both Bosniak and Croat and Serb, even Serb, protested. Then he gave a nationalistic, chauvinist speech saying that it was high time all Ustasha crimes against the Serbian people were avenged, and that all those Serbs who refused to join in this were traitors, and we would not regard them at all. Those who joined in, who joined him, started to insult the other Serbs calling them traitors and promising them revenge after they were back from Croatia, which created an overall atmosphere of mistrust between Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats because at this point, the JNA identified itself fully with the Greater Serbian and Chetnik aims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Colic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Pero Colic was and the Kozarac light brigade. Was that a unit stationed, or headquartered in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The unit in question, while it was deployed at the front line was, as far as I remember, quartered in Novska, in the theatre in Croatia. However, once the war in Croatia was over, it came back and was stationed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other JNA units were in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The 43rd, if my memory serves me right, the 43rd Brigade which was led by Colonel Arsic and Major Radmilo Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the actual headquarters of the 43rd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 43rd Brigade were in the barracks at Urija, which is a Prijedor neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if that unit was armed with any heavy weapons, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Both units were armed with various kinds of equipment, the kind of equipment that is most commonly used to arm a brigade, including artillery, which consisted of a number of tanks, guns, Howitzers, and, of course, the usual infantry weapons commonly used by the units of this size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja. Do you know where they are from?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel Arsic comes from Serbia. He's a Serb from Serbia proper. He comes from the area of Sumadija, judging by his accent, that is, the area of central Serbia. As for Major Zeljaja, he used to serve as a member of the military in the town of Sarajevo. He was in charge of the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the outbreak of the conflict, how many in your view, your estimate, what percentage of the officers and men in those units stationed in Prijedor were of Serb ethnicity? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Those units were -- those units consisted almost a hundred per cent of the members of the Serb community, with a negligible percentage of Bosniaks, Croats, and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the police force in Prijedor? How was that broken down as far as the ethnicity of its members?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The police force, as other major institutions within the country, was predominantly Serb traditionally speaking, although the composition of the Prijedor population, as I've already indicated, was equal, 50/50 between Serbs and Bosniaks. However, the police force had almost 80 per cent of members of the Serb community. And as regards major offices, major functions within the police, that was also the case. The similar situation prevailed in all other major state institutions. I'm referring to the judiciary, to the financial institutions, and other public companies and public institutions in the town of Prijedor, which was more or less the case with other major towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about the distributions of these top posts, you're speaking of before the 1990 elections. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go and talk about now those elections in 1990. Can you tell us what the results of those elections were in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Prijedor parliament had 90 seats, of which the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, received 30 at the multiparty elections. The opposition parties got a total of -- I'm referring to the Social Democratic Party, the Social Alliance, the Liberal Alliance, and the party of Mr. Murselovic, that is, the Party of Private Entrepreneurs, they had 30 deputies. The Serb Democratic Party had 28 seats, and the Croatian Democratic Union, 2 seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any kind of agreement on the republic level between the three national parties for the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an agreement which was signed by the presidents of the parties, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Karadzic, to the effect that the offices of the presidents of municipalities and chiefs of police in those municipalities were either SDA or HDZ or SDS. One should go to the party which had won the majority of seats. As for the offices of the deputies to these two functions, they were to go to the second party, that is, the party which had won the second largest number of votes. So specifically for the area of Prijedor, since the Party of Democratic Action got the majority of seats, in accordance with the said agreement, that party should have gotten the offices of the president of the Municipal Assembly and the chief of police. As for the Serb Democratic Party, they shall have received the offices of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly and the deputy chief of police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was considered the top position within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The top position within the municipality, or rather positions, were the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly, the vice-president of the municipality, the president of the municipal government, ministerial positions, that is, the offices of various secretaries within the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of these positions was considered the top position?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The top position was, of course, the position of the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who became the president of Prijedor municipality following the elections?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Following the elections, the president of Prijedor municipality was Mr. Muharem [as interpreted] Cehajic. He became the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that the -- you told us the results of the elections and that the SDA outpolled the SDS party in Prijedor. How did that compare to the results in other municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Bosnian Krajina, generally speaking, is an area which, according to the composition of its municipalities, is predominantly Serb with the exception of the municipalities of Prijedor and Sanski Most. The municipalities situated in the Sana River valley, Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Bosanski Novi, which all of whom had major concentrations of Muslim/Bosniak population. So in the town of Sanski Most, the Bosniak population was predominant. They had five -- they were 5 per cent more than the second largest group. But although there were more than 5 per cent more Bosniaks in Sanski Most, it was the SDS that won the election and not the SDA, as one would have expected in accordance with the composition of the population. Whereas in Prijedor, although the Serb leadership at Pale expected that, in view of the 1991 [as interpreted] Census, Prijedor was considered to be a predominantly Serb town, they thought that the election would be won by the SDS. But contrary to their expectations, it was the SDA that won the election in Prijedor. So apart from Jajce, which was geographically separated and situate towards the south of the country, Prijedor was the only town in which the SDA won the election, in that area of Bosnia. And I am referring to the Banja Luka region, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that the Serb republic leadership was surprised at the results, and the translation indicates "in view of the 1991 census." Which census were you speaking of, regarding the 1990 election results?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. 1981. It was either my mistake or an error in interpretation. I was referring to the census carried out in 1981, because that census, that is, the census in 1991, took place after the election which took place in 1990. So only the census of 1981 could be taken into consideration because the census which took place in 1991 occurred after the election, and it turned out that Prijedor was predominantly Muslim. But before that census had taken place, it was somewhat surprising that the Prijedor, being a predominantly Serb town, was now ruled by the SDA, that is, that the SDA won the election in Prijedor. I apologise, but I have to intervene in the interpretation. I would like the interpreters to interpret the word "Muslim" with the word "Bosniak." The word Muslim denotes religious affiliation, whereas Bosniak is a term that denotes an ethnic group. Muslims can refer to Albanians also, but the word "Muslim" should be interpreted as Bosniaks, because it refers to the Bosniak population, the Bosniak ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll try to do that, and I'll try to do that also, and please correct me if I don't. Sir, this victory for the SDA in Prijedor, did it have an effect on your personal standing on the level of the republic with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. republic-level SDA leadership and your popularity among Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As is usually the case, it is the winners who become popular amongst the population. So my popularity was the result of the fact that Prijedor was the only town where the SDA won the election in the Banja Luka region. This, later on, was instrumental in my being delegated to the republic level as a representative of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member, then, of the main board of the SDA party for the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: This was in 1990, and I was 28 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the SDS party react to the results of the elections in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The SDS thought that the elections were not regular. They expected a victory. So they lodged a number of complaints with the election commission. And after these complaints had been reviewed by this commission, the republic commission, it was established that the results of the election were legal and regular, and that the procedure, the whole procedure, was performed in a regular way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the agreement to divide positions. Can you tell us if there were any problems in Prijedor implementing that agreement between the three national parties?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The representatives of the SDS had a difficult time reconciling with the fact that they had lost the elections in Prijedor and that a certain number of very important positions which, so far, were traditionally Serb positions or belonged to the members of the Serb community, they expected that they would only strengthen their position in the town. But now, those positions were supposed to go to the SDA party, so they tried to obstruct the results -- the implementation of the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally involved in the negotiations regarding the division of positions in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point did the leader of the SDS party intervene in the negotiations, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Since even after almost two months, the local government in Prijedor was still not established, and since the town was in crisis because the SDS did not wish to implement the results of the elections, Radovan Karadzic became personally involved. At one point in time, he invited me to have a talk with him after one of the sessions of the BH parliament, together with Mr. Srdjo Srdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Srdjo Srdic's position at the time that you had that talk with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, Srdjo Srdic was the president of the Serbian democratic party, and a deputy to the Chamber of Citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So basically, his position was very similar to mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those negotiations, what did the national agreement call for, and can you explain the positions of the various -- of yourself and Mr. Mr. Srdic in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of each such talk, I advocated the position that we should implement the results of the elections. Initially, I thought -- I believed, and this was our initiative, that all parties should be made part of the process, including the opposition parties, and that they should all participate in the local government. I thought that this would create a more stable position, a more stable government, for the municipality of Prijedor, which was severely opposed by the SDS, and in particular, Mr. Srdjo Srdic. We then made a second proposal. They insisted that the opposition parties should not be part of -- should not participate in the government. Then we proposed that the positions should be distributed amongst the three parties, the SDA, the HDZ, and SDS, in accordance with the election results, which again was rejected by the delegation of the SDS and Mr. Srdjo Srdic, implying and alluding to the fact that the SDA had 32 seats within the parliament and HDZ only 2 which, for them, meant that they would constitute a minority, that the Serbs would be a minority within that government because they thought that the other two parties would probably try to form a coalition, which was not specifically stated by them at the time but which later became to be known as an Ustasha/Muslim coalition. Our next proposal was that the government should be divided 50/50, that the SDS would get 50 per cent of the seats and the SDA also 50, which was a concession for the SDS. And then that the SDA should allocate a certain number of positions to the HDZ. With these concessions to the SDS, we wished to create a balance and a stable political situation in the municipality. But this, again, was rejected by the SDS, and then the conversation, the talk with Mr. Karadzic followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break now. The trial stands adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And we can continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I want to regress a moment and go back to talking about the JNA. Was there an incident in 1991 where a JNA unit passed through Prijedor that received some publicity in which you were involved?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, I think probably August or late July, I was at work. I was practicing medicine, and a number of citizens, in a very agitated state of mind, told me that several tens of JNA tanks passed through Prijedor. Their agitation was easy to understand,, in view of the ongoing war in the neighbouring Croatia. Prijedor was only 30 kilometres far from Croatia. I drove in a car with several citizens to see what was going on, and I could see that in the Prijedor airport, Urije, there were between 20 and 30 tanks stationed there. When I talked to several officers to tell me what was going on, they either did not want to offer an explanation or simply didn't know. They said that only their superior, General Uzelac, had the authority to speak about that because he was in command of the operation. On my way back, I saw a car in which I noticed a very high-ranking officer. I motioned with my hand, and the car stopped. I came out of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. car. I approached the other car. And out came a colonel who said his name was Colonel Kostic, who was the chief of the intelligence service, of the military intelligence service of the Banja Luka corps. In my role as a deputy and on behalf of the parliament, I requested him to provide an explanation as to what was going on to help allay the tensions, rising, mounting among the citizens at that point. He replied that the army did not have any obligation to account for anything, that the only place they can be called to account for something was in Belgrade. I then told him that the army should be under the control of civilian authorities, and that their responsibility was not only to the general staff but also to organs of civilian authority. The parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina was, according to the constitution, the highest body, the highest authority, so the least to be expected at that point was to have information provided on what was going on. In the contrary case, the implication would be that Yugoslavia at that point was based on dictatorship-like relations, like a military junta, without any power for civilian authorities. His reply was rather abrupt. He said that he wished to discuss with me no further, and that's how our conversation ended. Deputy Srdjo Srdic, before I managed to explain what was going on, in the parliament, he came forward accusing me of having been very arrogant. He said I arrogantly asked questions about something that, in his view and in his words, was not within my competence. Then I came forward, took the floor, and explained that I merely requested information from the army, so that I could go out to the citizens and explain to them what was going on. The army completely ignored my request, and I'm not speaking of myself as myself personally, Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, but rather as a deputy member of parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This caused -- gave rise to a number of different reactions in the parliament. Representatives of the SDS reacted in a very negative way -- there was an uproar -- while members of other parties approved my reaction. This indicated the attitude of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the JNA. It was divided on that issue, just like all Yugoslav citizens were divided at that time into two camps, two factions, pro-Milosevic and anti-Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this exchange at the parliament and the speech of Srdic televised?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both speeches, both mine and that of Mr. Srdic were televised, so that citizens throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina had the opportunity to listen to both these discussions in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the Territorial Defence forces and the fact that there was a change in their organisation -- and correct me if I am wrong, but I believe you testified this morning about the JNA taking control of the weapons of the Territorial Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's true of all the republics of the former Yugoslavia with the exception of Slovenia. In all of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, the JNA took all the weapons in possession of the Territorial Defence units which were as much as republican armies. They took all the weapon from the storage facilities, both light and heavy weapons, and transferred them to their own storage facilities. The only place where they failed to do so was in Slovenia, because the Slovenian authorities prevented this in good time and prevented them being transferred to the JNA storage facilities from their own facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, was there an occasion in Prijedor where some of these or some weapons were distributed by the JNA back to TO units?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. During 1991, a part of the weapons in possession of the Prijedor Territorial Defence was distributed throughout the local communes of Prijedor municipality. These are small territorial entities. There were around 70 of these in the Prijedor municipal area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what events had triggered that distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: This was on Colonel Arsic's initiative. As a representative of the SDA, I was invited to a meeting -- excuse me if I'm using a term which is not adequate, but I think this was the council for national defence of Prijedor municipality, presided by the president of the municipality and attended by chief of police, chief commander of the Territorial Defence, commander of the civilian protection. We were also invited to these meetings as party presidents. Mr. Miskovic, who was then serving as party president, Mr. Arsic and Mr. Zeljaja were also present as representatives of the army. The session was chaired by the then president of the municipality, Mr. Cehajic. The explanation for this sort of initiative was provided by Colonel Arsic. He said that there was a certain danger that the so-called Zenga which is how they referred to Croatian soldiers of the then Croatian army, there was a danger that those could cross from Croatia into Prijedor municipal area, the front line as I've said before was very near. What triggered this is an incident in which five soldiers crossed from -- into the neighbouring municipality Bosanska Dubica to the village of Knezevica only 50 kilometres from Prijedor which caused fear especially among the Serbian population. So the distribution of these weapons took place following an explanation that the population had to be protected from incursions by Croat paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was this distribution of weapons done equally in all of the various settlements of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, it was not distributed evenly or adequately in all places. We were informed that some local communes with Muslim majority, Bosniak local communes, in some of these, weapons were distributed that were antiquated, wrong type of ammunition was distributed. Some handheld launchers with no cartridges, quite useless. On the other hand, in other local communes of Serb majority, the situation was different. In some local communes, there were complaints that less weapons were given out than in those local communes where Serbs were the majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about attending a meeting of an institution that was translated as the national defence council. Is that an institution that was provided for under the existing law in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and can you briefly explain the purpose of that institution?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The council for national security was designed to function in the immediate threat of war. And of course, in war danger. By virtue of his function, the president of that council is also the president of the municipality, and he's also the civilian commander of the defence of the town. And according to law, he's responsible for the defence of the town on the local level. So both the chief of police and the commander of the civilian protection and the defence, Territorial Defence, are all under his authority. And also, in terms of, not really immediate command subordination but in a certain sense, he was also the superior of the army that was in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the law provide that the chief of police and the army commander in that area would also be members of this institution, the national defence council, on the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence, yes. As far as the army commander, specifically in this case, Colonel Arsic, according to Bosnian and Herzegovinian law was supposed to be present, but that was not binding for him. So it was not binding, but in practice, that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your experience up until the -- during your presence in the municipality in 1992, did you see evidence of cooperation between the army and particularly Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja and authorities from the SDS political party?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Although I sensed or intuited, and many people on the ground came back to me with this sort of information, but I was still very reserved for quite a while, because the JNA itself, despite all the changes that I had described, declared itself publicly as the Yugoslav People's Army and wanted to have nothing to do with any national allegiances. So the information I received at the beginning, I was quite reserved. But then in early 1992, February 1992, March 1992, more specific information followed from people who saw JNA lorries in Serbian villages where weapons were being distributed by JNA soldiers and were in certain places such as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. above the village of Brezicani, where there were reports about the existence of training grounds for Serbs. And these training grounds were controlled by the JNA. At that point, I felt the need to draw Colonel Arsic's attention to these facts. When I told him about it, he said he thought this was not true. And although I had no photographs at that time, I used a trick. I told him that we had photographs of this at our disposal. He was then confused, and he said, "Well, okay, we'll look into the matter then. Maybe some irresponsible officer did something like this, but we'll certainly look into this matter."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Skipping ahead just for a moment, after the takeover of the municipality and the removal of the legally elected government from the 1990 elections, did you see evidence of cooperation between the army and the new authorities of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period when the military, the so-called military putsch took place in Prijedor, that is, when the army had the legal organs of authority dismissed, that's the night between the 30th of April and the 1st of May, the next morning, so on the 30th of April, that is, on the 1st of May, we found the whole town flooded with military. In front of all important town institutions, there were patrols, between 10 and 15 soldiers as in classical war films where the military putsch takes place, outside the police station, outside the municipal building. But on that day, Colonel Arsic officially distanced himself from this act. He said these were -- this had been done by paramilitary units of the SDS. However, it was abundantly clear that this was merely an anti-declaration, and that this was not true because citizens recognised soldiers from his brigade, or the brigade under the command of Colonel Colic among the soldiers standing outside these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd now like to briefly play a portion of Exhibit S11, a video. And on the transcript of that, I'd like to play the portion on page 2 starting with the announcer's statement by Rade Mutic, and have that played and translated up to the response to the questions from the journalist and the response from the guest, and then stop the videotape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, do we have the transcript, the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's Exhibit 11A. Perhaps I could give my transcript to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we need three, for three booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Looking for a solution. I don't think -- could the interpreters read off the -- they can't watch the ELMO because the video will be on. We could come back to it later after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have another copy here with the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would two copies be sufficient. If the interpreters are ready, we can start the playing of the video. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] We called him from Prijedor as he is at the moment the person the best informed on events in Prijedor. For already two months there have been fights with Muslim extremist in the territory of the Prijedor municipality. For almost two months the town was quiet but the town's surroundings were not. This was affirmed these days. For the last three days, there are fights again. Can you explain to us how, why? First of all, one remark. It's not only me being the best informed on events in Prijedor. All authorities and their bodies are very well familiarized with events in Prijedor, and as I, maybe more than the others, cooperate with them, I am familiar as well. Answering the question about my opinion on fights in the last two months in the territory of Prijedor municipality, they are not only in the territory of Prijedor municipality. There are fights, more or less, fierce in all Western Krajinas municipalities. Firstly, and it is known in public, Muslim extremists attacked our units in Hambarine and Kozarac, and this was the cause for what happened. We were not naive to think that combat actions will not repeat. We were ready to meet the same attacks by Ustashas and extremists and Muslim fundamentalists. And it happened these days. The fights in Rizvanovici and Biscani are renewed, and at this moment, we are in the process of liberating the Kurjevo forest, including all inhabited areas there. In the first place, where the concentration of Muslim forces is great, especially after the withdrawal from Kozarac and Hambarine. One Prijedor's unit on the Posavina front line in the region of Gradacac. What is the situation there? We have a very difficult task, because the unit is deployed in the mountain, the rugged area where Muslim extremists are well fortified. But in spite of that, as I've said, when the unit was departing for the front line, they will carry out the tasks they have. There were days when they were passing seven or even more kilometres in a single day. Their performance is excellent."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise Colonel Arsic on that video?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised both the journalist and Colonel Arsic. The journalist is Mutic, and the soldier is Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Colonel Arsic said -- and I don't have the transcript in front of me at the moment, but to paraphrase -- that "all of the -- it's not only me being the best informed on events in Prijedor, all authorities and their bodies are very well familiarized with events in Prijedor as I, maybe more than others, cooperate with them." Is that consistent with what you experienced and saw in Prijedor regarding the relationship between Colonel Arsic and the authorities that took over power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in this way that Colonel Arsic wanted to emphasise that the responsibility for certain events was not only his, but that in fact, members of government bodies were the people who were familiar with what was going on. But in fact, he said that certain orders, although he didn't say this expressly, but from a number of other events, it was clear that some orders came from the civilian authorities of Prijedor as well as certain instructions to certain units of the JNA and Territorial Defence and police in Prijedor municipality, which he implicitly confirmed with this statement of his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to our discussion before the break, we were talking about the division of posts, and you mentioned an incident at the parliament where you had a discussion with Mr. Karadzic. Can you tell us about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the last part of your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what happened when you had the conversation with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I said that the meeting was initiated by Mr. Karadzic himself, but was probably the result of the complaints of the president of the SDS and the leadership of the SDS on the SDA leadership. At least, this is what I could gather from his words. Their leadership accused us , blamed us for the failure of the agreement. And I said that we had made several concessions to the SDS in order to reach an agreement on several occasions, and that we were in favour of such an agreement and that we wanted a more peaceful and more stable situation in the area of the municipality. And that is what I told explicitly Mr. Karadzic. I remember telling him that we tried to reach a solution, a peaceful solution, but that the three proposals failed. He was very surprised. It was obvious that he had had some different information. And throughout that conversation, he tried to be as friendly and polite as possible. And he tried to alleviate the situation which was obviously very difficult and problematic. He even made a joke at one point, but one of his sentences, which was uttered in a facetious manner could be interpreted as some kind Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of warning. When I said that we would agree with the option where the SDS would have 50 per cent of the seats and the SDA, which had the majority, together with the HDZ would have only 50 per cent in order to reach an agreement, and I thought that we demonstrated a considerable amount of understanding by giving that proposal, he laughed. He smiled, and he said: "Be careful with my people. Be careful with Serbs, because if they get angry, they can be very difficult."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following these conversations, were there negotiations on the local level to try to actually divide up each of the posts?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I forgot to mention that I had said to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Srdic during that meeting that I, personally, as the president of the party, agreed with the proposal, but that I had to put it before our main board and that I needed an approval for the proposal from the leadership in Sarajevo as well, because there was a general agreement at the level of the republic which was somewhat different from the proposal that I had made in order to reach an agreement. And thanks to a number of people who were quite understanding, I managed to convince them that this was necessary and that the objectives would be served in the best way by proceeding like that. And that was how the agreement was then carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, the conversation you had with Karadzic, did that take place at the parliament in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a semi-formal conversation during one of the breaks in the session of the parliament. Mr. Jovo Tintor, a very close associate of Mr. Karadzic invited me to join Mr. Karadzic who at the moment was together with Mr. Srdjo Srdic in the lobby of the parliament building. And it was after this invitation that we had this talk in the presence of Mr. Tintor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to make sure we understand the agreement you proposed, you proposed that the SDS, which had received 28 seats, would receive half the positions, and that the SDA party, which had 30 seats, would receive half the positions by give some of its positions to the HDZ party which had two seats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: That is correct, though I wanted to indicate that I did not wish this type of agreement to imply any link of the SDA and the HDZ, though there was a danger of such an interpretation, that there was an agreement between the SDA and the HDZ. But we in the territory of the Prijedor municipality, always endeavoured to apply the principle of equidistance in our political actions, that there was always the same distance between the SDS and the SDA, and the SDA and the HDZ. However, because of that conviction of the SDS, we finally agreed to this proposal, but we made it clear that did not imply any specific link that we might have had with the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain why did you want to avoid the appearance that the SDA and HDZ were in alliance in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, the population of the Potkozarje area had suffered a lot during the Second World War and were the victims of the Ustasha regime in the territory of the Prijedor municipality. Many Serbs, even women and children, were taken to concentration camps in Croatia, and they had painful memories from that period of time. So given this historical burden, we wanted to demonstrate an equal amount of cooperation with both sides, because Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a country, was constituted on the basis of this principle, the principle of cooperation between the three ethnic groups. Any alliance of any of the two ethnic groups would cause -- would entail destabilisation of the country and eventually lead to disintegration of the country. One of our primary objectives was to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina the way it was, and with that in mind, we tried to retain this equidistance between the SDA, SDS, and HDZ, to the extent it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have shown to the witness Exhibit S97B. If that could be given to the witness to review.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, have you had a chance yesterday to briefly review this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have briefly. This document is a rather detailed description of the division of power in the territory of the Prijedor municipality, including a number of significant political functions and major public institutions which fell under the jurisdiction of the municipal government. The proposal was drafted by a group of people. You can see my signature on one of the pages -- on only one of these documents. The remaining documents have been signed by a person whose signature I cannot identify at this point because the participants in these negotiations were not the same all the time. I have to point out that nothing, none of the conclusions indicated in these documents have ever been implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the document please be put on the ELMO for a short moment in time because it was not announced as a exhibit in connection with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no. Therefore, my request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Doctor, that this consists of -- I don't want to take the time to count now, but more than ten pages detailing specific positions such as reading from the second page the 4th of July company that the director would be SDA and deputy director SDS, that the Toplana company, the director would be SDS, deputy director SDA, et cetera, for many positions throughout Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There were such proposals. There were many such proposals. This is only one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, looking at the third page, there are proposals for the court?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: This is page 2. It would be page 4 in B/C/S, titled "Justice Department". I believe that is the question that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just read the names of the positions that were being assigned or divided in the justice area.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The basic court or the lower court and the president of the Court, public prosecutors' office, the lower public prosecutors' office, deputy public Prosecutor, and one more deputy public Prosecutor. As you can see, there were two deputies to the public Prosecutor, one of the posts being intended for the HDZ. Then we have the municipal public attorney's office, municipal public attorney, deputy municipal public attorney, and municipal misdemeanours court, and the office of the president of the Court. So in total, that would be eight or ten key positions within the justice department in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to go to what is page 8 on the English translation, but the page entitled "Public Security." And just to speed things up, I'll read the names of the positions. It indicates the Prijedor public security station, the chief of the station, the general police commander, deputy commander, assistant for the -- word is illegible. Assistant for crime, assistant for traffic, traffic police commander, deputy commander, assistant commander, then the head of crime division, the assistant for white-collar crime, assistant for general crime, the head of legal affairs, the head of communication, the head of material equipment department. And then below the public security heading is a heading Prijedor Territorial Defence staff, and it indicates the TO staff commander. Is it correct that there was discussion regarding the division of all of these post inside the justice, public security, and TO, and who would be nominated for these positions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: There was no discussion regarding specific names.
