What was discussed was the possibility of bringing these offices in line with the results of the elections and that with time, the national -- the ethnic composition of the police force should be changed, once again in accordance with the ethnic makeup of the population and the results of the elections. But of course, we were perfectly aware of the fact that this would take time, maybe even years, and no one insisted on any dismissals from the police force, only with the purpose of changing the national -- the ethnic structure of the police force. Since 80 per cent of the police functions were occupied by members of the Serb community, we proposed, we suggested that the long-term objective would be that once a specific Serb police officer retires, then a new Bosniak police officer would be hired. The overall objective being to have this structure of the police force be reflective of the overall ethnic makeup of the community. So out of all these top positions that you have enumerated, eight or ten positions, as far as I know, only one position went to a Bosniak. So by asking for at least three more positions, we tried to strike a balance within the leadership of the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in the negotiations, specific names were not mentioned. How did you actually arrive at a name? Let's take the position of the chief of the police station. Who got that position, and can you explain to us who proposed that person?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The position of the commander of the Territorial Defence and the chief of police force, together with a number of positions within the justice department, have a two-level type of subordination. In practice, de facto, these people were nominated by the local level of government. These people are -- their names are put forward. In the case of the chief of the police, by the SDA of Prijedor to the minister, and it is the minister who, de jure, in accordance with law, approves of the nomination or appointment. But this is only in principal. In practice, he should always approve the proposal that comes from the local level. So all of these nominations to all of the posts that I have enumerated, the chief of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police, the commander of the Territorial Defence and the various judiciary functions, are all discussed and proposed at the local level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, what you explained -- you were talking about the chief of police. Is it also correct, the same thing, for the Territorial Defence and for the president of the Court, the ministry of justice, the Territorial Defence at the republic level would have to, de jure, approve those nominations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, the same principal being applied to the judiciary, to the Territorial Defence, to the secretary for national defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of Prijedor after the 1990 elections, who did the SDA nominate for the chief of police position?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Talundzic a professional policeman, prior to that nomination?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The position of the chief of police is a political position, so in practice, both the chief of police and his deputy are politicians. The remaining positions within the police force that you indicated are positions which required previous experience in the police work, which is not the case, in principle, for the chief of police and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct that Mr. Talundzic was not a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was an engineer who was employed in the Ljubija mine ore company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular problem with a deputy police commander proposed by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The post of the deputy police commander went to the SDS. However, on two occasions, nominations were sent to Sarajevo which were not adequate because nominations were sent in respect of individuals who only had secondary education. But the law required a university degree for anyone occupying the post of chief of police or deputy chief of police. And the SDS accused the SDA, and me personally, for not letting the nominated deputy chief of police. And that is the reason why they did not want to discuss the remaining eight positions within the police force which were important. And in this way, they obstructed any changes -- all changes from taking place within the police force, and they accused us of obstructing this process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving from Prijedor back up to the level of the republic and events leading to Bosnian independence, can you describe the process by which the Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, the entire Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia, was divided in two camps, pro- and anti-Milosevic. A number of events occurred which eventually led to the dissolution of Yugoslavia, Slovenia having been the first republic to secede, which was followed by Croatia, and then it was Bosnia's turn. Bosnia and Herzegovina had to make a decision. They had to decide whether to remain within the rump Yugoslavia or Greater Serbia, or to follow the example of the two previous republics and call a referendum with the objective of deciding whether Bosnia and Herzegovina should go independent, as Slovenia and Croatia. As for the Croatian Democratic Union and the Croatian ethnic group, the answer was a foregone conclusion because it was obvious that the HDZ and the Croatian population within Bosnia and Herzegovina would vote for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its secession from Yugoslavia, following the example of Croatia. The HDZ and Croats in Bosnia generally speaking refused any possibility of staying within Yugoslavia. As for Bosniaks, their position was, as I have described, that we were not strongly opposed to any of the solutions. However, as I have already explained, with the departure of Croatia, there would no longer be appropriate balance within the rest of Yugoslavia, and we believed that the only solution that at the time was acceptable for Bosnia was that the issue of independence should be decided on a referendum. The matter was brought before the parliament which voted in favour of a referendum. The parliament decided that a referendum should be called, the question being: "Are you in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina." I must emphasise that the deputies of the Serb Democratic Party did not participate in this voting, which does not mean that other Serbs, members of other parties, did not participate in the voting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the referendum on independence held?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't remember the exact date. I think it was in late February or beginning of March. Beginning of March probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when Bosnia was recognised by the European Union and the United States as an independent country?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember clearly because it was associated with a number of other events. That took place on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking now about United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. That was quite a bit earlier. That was during April. What I was referring to was recognition by the United Nations. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Bosnia recognised by and admitted as a member of the United Nations? You mentioned it was associated with other events in Prijedor. Can you tell us what was going on when you heard the news that Bosnia had become admitted into the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: It was 7.00 in the evening. The event was televised on the 22nd of May, 1992. At that moment, I was in my parents' house, and I heard shots being fired. I went out of the house to see what was going on. Several hundreds metres from my parents' house, I saw people gathering. I approached them, and I saw that a group of people had gathered around several people who were lying on the ground and a white Lada car. I came closer to see what was going on, and I realised that two young men who were lying on the ground were fatally wounded. In fact, already dead. Three others were slightly wounded. One of them, as far as I can remember, was not even wounded. I think there were six of them all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this incident where the two men were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The incident took place at the Polje bus stop which belonged to the Hambarine local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated you came to the scene of this Hambarine incident on the 22nd of May. Were you there when the shots were actually fired?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- you indicated you heard the shots and went to the scene. About how far was it from your parents' house to where the car was and the men were dying?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As I said, I think several hundred metres. Possibly 3 or 400 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you got to the scene?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I acted as any physician would. I examined the wounded. I saw that two of them were dead, were shot dead, and that the remaining three were wounded with wounds that didn't pose a threat to their lives. But as I had no medical kit handy to administer medical care to the wounded, to the injured, I asked for emergency, for first aid, to be called for the wounded from a telephone in a local commune so that they could be assisted because regular phone lines unlike the one at the local commune were interrupted in that period. They were cut off. Also, another member of the Territorial Defence who was manning the checkpoint was wounded. Ferid Sikiric, he was wounded in the upper thigh a bit in the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you pointed to somewhere on your body. Could you stand up and just point to the area where you saw the wound on Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Sikiric's wound was approximately in this region. So we're talking about the part between the lumbar region and the gluteal region, the upper part of the upper leg, in this region here. Please excuse me if anyone should not understand medical terminology, the technical terms, but that's where the shot was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, would it be accurate to describe the area that the witness pointed at as just below the belt on the right leg, slightly posterior on the right side about 4 inches to the back in a posterior direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely agree with this description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that incident. I didn't mean to go into details with that now because it's out of sequence. But is it correct that this happened the same day that Bosnia was admitted into the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these movement [sic], as the events unfolded in 1991 with the war in Croatia, did it become apparent to people that Bosnia was moving in this direction, and was it an issue, the future independence of Bosnia, among the political parties?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period in 1990, 1991, or 1992? Could you specify, please? Or do you mean the entire period from the beginning all the way to the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to 1991, once the war in Croatia is going on. At that time, did it become apparent that Bosnia -- that certain parties were moving, the SDA in particular, towards seeking the independence of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At that time, our attitude was not so decided because the Croatian issue had not been decided yet. At the moment, when Croatia was recognised as an independent state, and as soon as it became clear that it had seceded from the former Yugoslavia, it was then that we realised we had no other way than to follow the same path.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late 1991 and early 1992, did the SDS respond to the events of the Croatian independence and the movements towards independence in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's slightly oversimplified to say it like that, but there was a whole sequence of complex events in Bosnia and Herzegovina culminating in the SDS leaving, walking out of the parliament. The republics of Slovenia and Croatia and even Macedonia made it very clear as early as 1991 to the federal government, which had made several intervention inside the monetary system up to that point violating principles embodied within the constitution, federal principles. Actually, this was done by Serbia as one single federal unit led by Milosevic. Croatia's and Slovenia's reaction was to stop sending federal revenue back to Serbia, back to Belgrade. No financial means or revenues that were related to the JNA were being sent. So I'm talking about the period before the official recognition of these two states as independent. In reply to Serbian incursions into the monetary system, they started to -- they started to print their own currency. The nature of these events was that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not remain aloof. The HDZ also insisted that Bosnia and Herzegovina speak out on these events. Our proposal was neutral. It was not as radical as the respective moves by Croatia and Slovenia. Our proposal was to establish a fund into which all the federal money would be pooled. So if Croatia and Slovenia at some later stage, in negotiating the way to continue with Yugoslavia, if they still decided to pool money into that fund, then Bosnia and Herzegovina would continue to do the same thing. But unless the agreement -- that this agreement was reached, then also we would keep the funds. So all the political parties in the parliament agreed, with the exception of the SDS, who categorically opposed any idea of stopping the money flow for the JNA or for Yugoslavia. This was not logical, however, because they were members of parliament of the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament and not of the Yugoslav parliament and also citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not Yugoslavia. A number of other events, which due to lack of time I will not go into now, culminated in the SDS walking out of the parliament. That's between 1991 and 1992, and they founded their own Serbian parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's please have a break now until 12.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. First of all, I have to apologise for being late. There was a serious problem in another section of our Trial Chamber. And in addition, I wanted to point out the confusion we had beforehand. It was only caused that you, of course, rightly mentioned that the document 97, it's provisional 97. And we, in our binder, still have the 65 ter numbers, and this was 76. Therefore, I would appreciate when coming back to these exhibits, please quote both the former 65 ter and the new provisional number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you talked about the walkout from the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the SDS party. Was that in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I think it was a little later. As far as I can remember, it was early 1992, the first days of January. The beginning of 1992 or possibly the end of 1991. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to responding by walking out of the parliament, were there efforts by the SDS to create regional organisations?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: These events followed before the SDS walked out of the parliament. This took place -- I can't say the exact date, but I think it was in the autumn of 1991, possibly October. October 1992 -- I'm sorry, 1991. The parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in session, and the media published the information that Autonomous Regions of Krajina, old Herzegovina, Romanija, and I can't remember. There was another autonomous region, had been established and marked off as autonomous Serbian regions. The only thing that struck us as suspicious is that some of the delegates from the SDS did not attend the session of the parliament. When the news came through the media, we were a bit taken aback by these events. And at that time, we were at a loss as to how to interpret the true reasons for the establishment of these regional structures or organisations. But immediately afterwards, the presidents of these autonomous -- of these regional structures spoke up and talked about the real intentions that they were harbouring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these regions created in all areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or were they created in particular areas of Bosnia, and did you notice the criteria that was used in selecting the areas for the autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The basic criterion was to do it in those areas of Bosnia and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Herzegovina where Serbs were the majority so that, for example, the region of Bosanska Krajina normally composed of about 60 per cent Serbs and 40 per cent non-Serbs was one of the largest such areas. And for the SDS, beyond doubt, among the most important regional organisations or parastate structures for the SDS, because Banja Luka was the centre of that region. The biggest town in Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serb majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Prijedor historically considered part of the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It has always been a part of the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any efforts made to have Prijedor join the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. At first, the reasons for the setting up of these regional structures were justified by economic reasons so that professors from the Banja Luka university came to explain that the only reason for the establishment of these regions was regionalisation, and that there was nothing else behind it, other than the idea of economic independence from Sarajevo. Our reply was logical; if that is really the case, then let's carve up the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina into regional units based on economic, and not ethnic principles, because these regional units that they had established were founded along national lines, and this was only applied in areas with Serb majority. Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, towns in which the SDS did not have more than 50 per cent majority, so could not vote to join the region of Banja Luka, they refused to join the autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January of 1991, was there a separation -- did the SDS set up a parallel organisation, parallel to the municipal government headed by Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As a result of the establishment of these autonomous regions and of the fact that a number of municipalities did not join the autonomous regions in which the Serbs were not the majority, the result was the establishment of the so-called Serbian municipalities, and that's what happened in Prijedor also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when that happened in Prijedor, the month and year?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I think that one such municipality was publicly proclaimed in January or February 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who became the president of that parallel government, the Serb municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The president of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor was Mr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Milomir Stakic prior to the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did know each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Above all, we were in the same line of work. But even prior to that, we often travelled together from Banja Luka to Prijedor on the train. That's about 60 kilometres. As he lived in Omarska, which was about halfway between Banja Luka and Prijedor, he used to get off at the Omarska train station. So we shared some time, and we talked long before these events. When he was a student at the medical school in Banja Luka, we went to the same school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what political party or political parties Dr. Stakic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in Omarska, the first party that was founded was the Serbian Radical Party, which was the only branch of the Serbian Radical Party throughout the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The headquarters of this party was in Belgrade. And it seems interesting that it was exactly in Omarska that they had the only branch in Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to my information, Mr. Stakic was also involved in the setting up of the Serbian Radical Party. But during the pre-electoral period, the Serbian Radical Party entered an electoral coalition with the Serbian Democratic Party, so that Mr. Stakic later, or perhaps even during the pre-electoral period, became a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the 1990 elections, was Dr. Stakic elected to the assembly, and did he gain any position in the government, in the legally elected government?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic was legally elected as a deputy in the municipal parliament in Prijedor and also legally elected as the deputy president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 93, which has the 65 ter number of 21. That could be put on the ELMO for the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you had -- Doctor, have you had a chance to read this brief document, and can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Would my learned colleague lay a foundation for these questions, whether this witness has ever seen this document prior to this event. Because he's a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us how you understand this document? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, although the image is not very clear, if I may, I'd like to have a look at the original document or the copy directly. All right. Now, the image is clearer so I can see very well. This is a document showing the decision to elect representatives for the annual BH-SDS convention in July 1991. Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kurnoga, and Duskovinovic [phoen] were elected by the municipal board of the SDS as candidates for the assembly, for the Bosnia-Herzegovina assembly of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to show the witness Exhibit 94, which had the 65 ter number of 25. Actually, I think we could put the English on the ELMO, and I believe the doctor is capable of understanding that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have the same objections, and not to be repetitious, we object every and single document on which does not appear the signature of this witness. So just for the record. We'll clarify these matters during our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But you will understand that for the same reasons, your objection is dismissed. But admittedly, I would prefer if at the end of such a statement, the witness could be asked whether or not he can identify the signatures of the persons on the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise this document as the minutes of a meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party in Prijedor on the 11th of September, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If you look at the document, it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page -- the bottom of page 3, the top of page 4 of the English translation, is it correct that it indicates that a vote was held for the position of vice-president of the party? A vote first for the president, and then the vice-president of the party?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were informed. I knew this even without looking at this document, because we were directly and indirectly informed about the elections in the SDS and that there were changes as concerns the position of the president and vice-president. We did have interparty negotiations, and it was crucial to know who the new representatives of the SDS would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were elected in the positions of president and vice-president of the SDS party in Prijedor at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, Simo Miskovic was elected president of the SDS, and Dr. Milomir Stakic was appointed vice-president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to now show the witness S96, which has the 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we please stop one moment that we don't get confused. We have in the B/C/S version, if the usher could please present the B/C/S version, we have a handwritten part. And I don't know, at the end is this a signature or what it is. It's the page ending with the number 595.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an electoral assembly, and the electoral procedure is usually like that. And as can be seen from this document, these rules were respected by the SDS. The electoral procedure was governed by an independent body meaning people who were not themselves be appointed, and the records, as the final document, were certified and confirmed by people who were not themselves appointed. It is obvious that the record was compiled by two persons. I think the first signature is Vojnovic, Ilija, and the second Ilindzic, Dragan. These persons were not, in a manner of speaking, involved in the procedure. They just put a stamp on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I perhaps think Mr. Lukic and perhaps the witness could help me. I believe that only the handwritten notes are translated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was the additional problem. I wanted to come to this later. Please, the last question, have you ever seen before the signatures of the two persons in the two bottom lines of the just-mentioned page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have never seen these two signatures before. I simply read on the left-hand side, quite legible in Cyrillic there are the names of these two people. I know both of them by sight. They're no personal acquaintances, and I have never seen their signatures before. I was not able to identify their signatures. I merely read their names on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. And if the usher could then please put on the ELMO the following two pages in Cyrillic, but not handwritten but machine-typed. Could you identify this document? This is probably just a summary of that what we found before as handwritten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. This is a summary from the Prijedor SDS meeting, pre-electoral meeting. That's precisely what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you identify on the second page, the last line and the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have here two different names. On the left is the person who chaired the electoral session. His -- Savanovic, Dragan, whom I know personally, and the other person is the recording clerk, Vinko Kos, whom I also know personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have before us a document without a signature at the left-hand side. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And my question is just here evidently the document tells us that the session was finalised at 19.30, and in the document before, it states 20.20. Therefore was my question, how is it possible to have this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have a look at the previous document. Your Honour, President of the Court, as you can tell, if you compare the first two pages of both records, you will see that both records have completely identical dates and time given for the beginning of the sessions. So 11th of September, 1991, 5.30 in the afternoon, both bearing the same title. These are minutes from the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor SDS. I'm afraid that maybe you're not able to read Cyrillic, so it's difficult, then, to assess the authenticity of these two documents in terms of their identity. But in abridged minutes, mistakes like these were often made because the level of organisation of parties such as the SDS at that point probably did not involve any professional assistance in terms of compiling records and minutes. So I believe this is an accidental mistake and not a deliberate one, but I think that yes, these two are identical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. Please proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to Exhibit S96, 65 ter number 69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could put, perhaps, on the ELMO the page with the stamped number ending in 8529, the B/C/S version ending in 8529 on the stamp in the lower right. Doctor, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I must point out that I haven't had an opportunity of seeing this document. However, we were informed of the contents of this document through the media in Prijedor in 1992 in the month of January when this happened. A moment ago, I couldn't remember the exact date. Now I see that it happened in January 1992. I remember quite clearly that when the decision of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor was reached, that is, the decision of the previously established Serbian municipality on the joining of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor with the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina. The document is signed by Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so -- to be clear for the record, when you say it's signed by Stakic, do you really -- are you familiar enough with his signature to recognise it, or are you stating that because that's the name underneath the signature line?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: In this case, I'm able to recognise the signature because I was able to see his signature not only the documents emanating from the SDS, but also on various kinds of medical -- medical documents such as prescriptions which he used to sign, the documents which normally circulated within the medical institutions and would sometimes reach me. So I am able to recognise the signature of Dr. Stakic at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to show the witness S101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can the parties agree that for clarification, not confusion, when there are additional questions, they be put immediately? If the witness could be shown, please, the document once more in B/C/S, in the English translation after the date, we don't have a word but apparently in the B/C/S version there is a word. Could you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please be of assistance, what you can see there? After 17 January, it's a question mark, 1992, and then the word afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word is customarily written or spelled in accordance with the rules of what was then called Serbo-Croatian language, or the Bosnian language, that after the number indicating the year, the word indicating the year would also follow. So translated into English, it would be 17 January, the date, and then the year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then we had on Friday a short discussion on the third page which ends with 96A. Do you know a Mr. Boro Bizgojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Boro Piskojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I misspelled the name, if the usher could present the third page after the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the gentleman in question is Mr. Blagojevic, who I didn't know. The word is misspelled. Obviously, this is Mr. Blagojevic. I had only heard of him, but I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness S101, which has the 65 ter number of 84.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: This is a decision on the election of deputies to the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, and the text goes on as follows: "By secret vote out of several candidates, the following were elected as deputy, Milomir Stakic, Milan Kovacevic, Milan Pelinovic, Simo Drljaca, Dusan Kurnoga, Simo Miskovic, Dragan Siljak." The document is once again signed by Mr. Milomir Stakic, in his capacity as the president of the Serbian people's assembly, that is, the Serbian municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'm finished with the documents for now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, from your viewpoint. Back in late 1991, early 1992, did you become concerned that an armed conflict or a war was coming to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I personally was rather worried with the way the events were developing generally in the former Yugoslavia, the federal level, because it was clear that Bosnia and Herzegovina would find itself in a very difficult situation in view of its multiethnic character. Also, in view of the fact that it's western borders were with the part of Croatia which, at the time, was already a war zone. I am referring to the Serbian autonomous region within the Republic of Croatia where conflicts had already started. But even before that, on the basis of certain developments within the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was clear that certain political differences which were quite significant between the SDS deputies and all other deputies to the parliament, let me mention only one example. At the first session, it was necessary to take a solemn oath, solemn declaration, as it is customary in all parliaments in the democratic world. So the text of the oath, and I'm paraphrasing now was "I pledge my loyalty, my allegiance to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." The SDS deputies insisted that the word order should be changed and that instead of "I pledge allegiance to the Republic of Yugoslavia" the text should be I pledge my loyalty to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and then to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This seems like a rather banal and perhaps not too difficult a political problem. However, the whole of the first session was spent discussing this seemingly banal issue which was actually very important because when the first law was supposed to be passed by the parliament, the law on the extension of additional taxes of 3 per cent to -- for the budget of the Yugoslav People's Army, a major split occurred. The SDS were in favour of prolonging this law. We tried to find a compromise, but the SDS members, deputies, were adamant in their proposal that we should continue supporting the JNA by acting like this. We tried to find a different solution. And again, the whole session was spent discussing this particular issue. And as time went by, the conflicts within the parliament regarding similar issues were getting exacerbated, and it became obvious that there was a major rift between the SDS and the remaining parties which were represented in the parliament. So after the third session of the parliament, it became obvious that whenever political discussions end up in a deadlock, that as soon as political discussions end up in a deadlock, an armed conflict is likely to occur. And that is how all major armed conflicts always occur in the world. So as I say, it was very difficult to find an acceptable solution. It was clear that Slovenia and Croatia were leaving Yugoslavia, and we all knew that an armed conflict as a result of that would occur in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon what you saw in the armed conflict in Croatia, did this cause you to have more concern about what an armed conflict would mean for Bosnia and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: We were worried for several reasons: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a multiethnic country; however, its multiethnic character is not the result of the mere fact that it is inhabited by Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. What further adds to the complexity of the issue is the fact that the population is mixed even in small villages. So it would be rather simple if Serbs only lived -- if one could say that Serbs lived in the western part, that is, the eastern part of the country, Croats in the western part of the country and so on and so forth. These three ethnic communities are mixed in all areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in the areas -- there were, of course, areas which had a predominant ethnic group. However, there were many other areas which were ethnically mixed, and it was impossible to envisage a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. One couldn't say where the front lines would be, and this is what we feared most at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your knowledge of the conflict in Croatia, did it appear that the civilian population suffered during that conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor, we were able to hear terrible stories about the events taking place in Croatia. Some of the stories were almost unbelievable, but I personally heard a story told by a soldier who had come back from the front line. Most of these stories were about the fact that these soldiers destroyed everything that came their way, even a story Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they played with a severed head of a man there and other gruesome incidents that I find very hard to describe here. At the time, I found difficult to believe these rumours because after all, we were part of Europe, living at the turn of the century, and we thought ourselves as part of the civilised world. There was a direct line connecting Stuttgart, Sarajevo, and the Adriatic coast, so we were closely linked with Europe, with the western Europe. And Bosnia-Herzegovina, we felt, was part of that world. On the other hand, this fact also instilled some hope in us. We didn't believe that such events would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, the reality in Croatia proved the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd now like to play a portion of 65 ter number 805, a video, if that brief portion could be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this will be Exhibit S117.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you could watch the screen while this video is played, I'll have some questions for you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I don't know if we need a translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise that scene, Doctor, and can you tell us, were you present when this speech was given? You have to answer out loud. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at that session. And now, as I was watching this, I was overwhelmed by the same feeling as then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the video, because we didn't have it translated, and forgive me -- and anyone correct me if I misstate, Dr. Karadzic indicated that the Muslims were not ready for war and could face extinction. Is that what you recall Dr. Karadzic saying at that session?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he said quite literally: "The road down which you are headed" so that's the road to have a referendum and go down the path of Bosnian and Herzegovinian independence, he said this road would lead Bosniaks to hell. Bosniaks are not ready for war. They are unarmed. They have no army. That road, he said, could lead to extinction for Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Dr. Karadzic said that the Muslims or Bosniaks were not ready for war, do you believe that's true, at least in regards to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Essentially, I think that was equally true in all parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not only in Prijedor. I know preparations carried out for the defence from a possible attack that might issue from such threats, Dr. Karadzic did say this sentence in public, but even prior to that, threats were coming from lower levels. This is only a threat coming from the very top, president of the SDS, about possible intentions by the SDS if we decided to still go down the road that could take the Bosniaks of Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell, as he said. Prijedor, like many other cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- I am referring to Bosniaks and Croats, not to Serbs now -- was not ready for defence, to defend itself from a possible attack by the SDS or the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with other individuals regarding how to possibly prepare the people of -- or the Bosniaks and non-Serbs, particularly the Bosniaks in Prijedor, for the possibility of a war?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: We, conscious as we were of the events in Croatia and the real danger for the war to spread, to spill over into Bosnia and Herzegovina, conscious as we were of the strength of the JNA, allegedly the fourth strongest military power in Europe at that point, the heavy weapons, the aviation, and all the other weapons they had, we did take certain steps, steps available to us at that moment, in order to prepare some sort of a defence to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe those steps that you took.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presidency took the decision that in the immediate threat of war, so we're talking about April 1992, throughout the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Territorial Defence units were to be set up. Also, even prior to that event, conscious as we were of the danger with the speech given by Dr. Karadzic and other lower-level delegates preceding even Karadzic's speech which was just the final confirmation of all our suspicions. All this led us to carry out certain preparations, political preparations, too, for people to understand that there was a real danger from the JNA because in the minds of most Bosniaks, the concept of Tito's Yugoslavia of the JNA, of World War II partisan past, all these had very positive connotations in their minds. Someone had to explain that this was no longer the JNA they knew, that this was the Serbian army posing a real danger to them. So this was the first problem we were facing. We had to explain these things to people. Another problem was how to organise these people. We didn't have any military structure at our disposals to use to organise ourselves. And a third and most serious problem is lack of weapons, because we didn't have any weapons or any serious weapons. To put up any serious form of resistance to a force such as the JNA then was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any obstacle to Bosnia obtaining weapons from third countries?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably you all know, but I'm going to repeat this: In the early stage of the war, there was a prohibition -- there was a ban on arms, so there was no legal way to import weapons. On the other hand, even prior to that ban, throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were joint patrols of the military and police. The whole country, ever since November or December, I think, 1991, was flooded by patrols, checkpoints being set up by the military and police jointly. That was because the army was accusing the parties of obtaining weapons. This was a way to control it. Between Banja Luka and Prijedor, for example, you can come across three, four, or more checkpoints on any of the important roads. It was absolutely impossible to transfer any considerable amount of arms into the country from any of the sides, because Bosnia was simply closed off in terms of communications from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that there was a ban and there was no legal way to import weapons, are you referring to an international embargo -- arms embargo on all the parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I would not like to broach here a major political issue relating to the import of weapons into the former Yugoslavia, but with Your Honours' permission, I will give my own opinion. Croatia was open to Hungary, Slovenia, and Italy. Serbia, that is representatives of the Serbian people, were armed directly by the JNA, which later was to proclaim itself Serbian army. And practically, the SDS had behind it the fourth military power in Europe, which one of the delegates once told me directly as we clashed in conversation. She said: "You Muslims, what do you think? We have behind us the JNA, a major military power. And what do you have? You have no backing. You have nothing." That was only one such comment that preceded the comments made by Mr. Karadzic later on. Talking about the ban, it actually only applied to the Bosniaks, because we were the only ones without weapons. So a ban on the import of arms could not be referring to either the Croatian or the Serbian side, speaking of sides. It only applied to the Bosniaks in practical terms, so we were the only side hit by the embargo, and there was no way for us to get weapons, no legal, or for that matter, illegal way, because due to these checkpoints being set up and Bosnia-Herzegovina being closed off from all sides, there was no way for us to get weapons into the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But just so the record is clear as far as the evidence, is it correct there was an international arms embargo upon all the states of the former Yugoslavia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have conversations with someone named Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who was Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic was an officer of the JNA, the former JNA. He was a major. And it was quite early, I think it was in spring 1991, as far as I know, he left the JNA, disappointed as he was by processes transforming the JNA into a Serbian army. Having realised that the events then taking place would lead to war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he placed himself at the disposal or - let me rephrase this, alongside with some other citizens and officers of Bosniak and other nationalities, as far as I can remember, these were not only Bosniaks - they set up or they called the Patriotic League and took as their platform the platform of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Just briefly, I will explain what this means, the platform of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This means that Bosnia and Herzegovina was in a situation where it would need to defend itself, and it calls on all those who feel that Bosnia and Herzegovina is their homeland and who see that Bosnia and Herzegovina is threatened by the JNA, all those who were patriots should return and defend their country. It struck me as logical. Mr. Halilovic was the president of the Patriotic League and a man who started and initiated a patriotic action to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Halilovic come to Prijedor, and did you have a discussion with him regarding what could be done to defend the people of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Halilovic came twice to Prijedor. The first time he came -- excuse me, I can't remember the exact date, but I think it was around September 1991. And he familiarized me with this platform of the presidency according to which the Patriotic League was to become an organisation, initially not a military organisation, but an organisation joined by all those who in the case of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina were willing to defend it. So he went around visiting people in the field who he thought would be willing to support the Patriotic League. We had a talk, and I also gave my support to this idea because I thought that it was necessary. The other time he came was, I think, November or December, so late in 1991. And that time, he was accompanied by another man whose name I cannot remember. The words he was using are -- he struck me as an officer probably, a military officer. This time, Mr. Halilovic wanted us to give our backing to the foundation of the Patriotic League in Prijedor municipality, which of course I agreed to. And we did support the foundation of the Patriotic League on the municipal level, also politically, above all politically, by politically mobilising a number of people, by explaining the ideas and aims behind the patriotic league.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid we have to call it a day for today. And the trial stands adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
